seo.shortDescription: Searchable U.S. duty table for all 124 HTS Chapter 76 aluminum lines: aluminum pays the 50% Section 232 tariff on its full value from every country (UK 25%), China 75%, Russia 200%, Canadian extrusions and tubes 100%. Scrap, powders and fasteners are outside Section 232.

overview.intro:
Chapter 76 covers aluminum: unwrought ingot, billet and slab (7601), scrap (7602) and powders (7603); the mill products made from them, extrusions, wire, sheet and plate, foil, tubes and fittings (7604–7609); and articles of aluminum, from windows and cans to cookware, cable, fasteners and castings (7610–7616). Base rates are low: **Free to 6.5%**, with 18 of the 124 lines Free.

What decides the cost is **Section 232**. Aluminum articles and most derivatives (92 lines) pay **an extra 50% of their full customs value** from every country (heading 9903.82.02), Canada, Mexico, the UAE, Bahrain and the EU included; household articles, ladders, blinds and luggage frames (15 lines) pay **25%** (9903.82.09). FTA and USMCA claims do not reduce it. The UK pays **25%** (15% on household articles) when the aluminum was smelted or most recently cast in the UK. Chinese aluminum pays another **25% under Section 301** (75% in total), Russian aluminum **200%**, and since September 15, 2026 **Canadian extrusions and tubes** (7604, 7608) pay a further **50% under Section 338**. Scrap, powders, large tanks, pot scourers, most fasteners and wire cloth (17 lines) are **outside Section 232**; most of them pay the 2026 Section 301 duties instead.

On top of the tariff, Commerce **antidumping and countervailing duty** orders cover aluminum extrusions and foil from China, common alloy sheet from China and 16 other countries, foil from five other countries and disposable aluminum containers from China. They are company-specific and not part of this table or the tariff calculator; see Tariff updates and Import documents.

productGroups.label: Unwrought aluminum (ingot, billet, slab)
productGroups.blurb: Primary and secondary aluminum in ingots, billets, sheet ingot (slab), foundry ingot, remelt scrap ingot and master alloys, non-alloyed or alloyed: 13 lines, Free to 2.6%. A Section 232 aluminum article: +50% from every country (UK 25% with UK-smelted or cast aluminum).

productGroups.label: Aluminum waste and scrap
productGroups.blurb: Aluminum waste and scrap: used beverage cans, wheels, turnings and other industrial and recyclable scrap: 5 lines, all Free. Outside Section 232 and on the 2026 Section 301 exemption list, so only China (25%, List 3) and Brazil (25%) pay extra.

productGroups.label: Aluminum powders and flakes
productGroups.blurb: Aluminum powders of non-lamellar structure and lamellar powders and flakes: 2 lines, 3.9% to 5%. Outside Section 232; they pay the 2026 Section 301 duty for most countries.

productGroups.label: Bars, rods and profiles (extrusions)
productGroups.blurb: Aluminum bars, rods and extruded profiles, hollow or not, non-alloyed or alloyed: 13 lines, 1.5% to 5%. +50% Section 232; Canadian extrusions also pay the 50% Section 338 duty since September 15, 2026. Chinese extrusions are under AD/CVD orders.

productGroups.label: Aluminum wire
productGroups.blurb: Aluminum wire, including wire rod in coils and alloy wire: 4 lines, 2.6% to 4.2%. +50% Section 232.

productGroups.label: Plates, sheets and strip (over 0.2 mm)
productGroups.blurb: Aluminum plate, sheet and strip thicker than 0.2 mm, including can body and lid stock: 19 lines, 2.7% to 6.5%. +50% Section 232. Common alloy sheet from China and 16 other countries is under AD/CVD orders.

productGroups.label: Aluminum foil (0.2 mm or less)
productGroups.blurb: Aluminum foil not over 0.2 mm, plain, rolled, backed or printed, including household foil and capacitor foil: 12 lines, Free to 5.8%. +50% Section 232. Foil from China, Armenia, Brazil, Oman, Russia and Türkiye is under AD/CVD orders.

productGroups.label: Tubes and pipes
productGroups.blurb: Aluminum tubes and pipes, seamless or not, of non-alloyed or alloyed aluminum: 4 lines, 5.7%. +50% Section 232; Canadian tubes also pay the 50% Section 338 duty since September 15, 2026.

productGroups.label: Tube or pipe fittings
productGroups.blurb: Aluminum tube or pipe fittings (couplings, elbows, sleeves): 1 line, 5.7%. +50% Section 232.

productGroups.label: Structures, doors, windows and frames
productGroups.blurb: Aluminum structures and parts: doors, windows and their frames, thresholds, roofing, siding, gutters, architectural work and mobile homes: 7 lines, 5.7%. A Section 232 derivative: +50%.

productGroups.label: Reservoirs and tanks (over 300 l)
productGroups.blurb: Aluminum reservoirs, tanks and vats of more than 300 liters, not fitted with mechanical or thermal equipment: 2 lines, 2.6%. Outside Section 232; they pay the 2026 Section 301 duty for most countries.

productGroups.label: Casks, drums, cans and boxes (up to 300 l)
productGroups.blurb: Aluminum casks, drums, cans, boxes and collapsible tubes of 300 liters or less, including beverage and aerosol cans: 6 lines, Free to 5.7%. A Section 232 derivative: +50%.

productGroups.label: Containers for compressed or liquefied gas
productGroups.blurb: Aluminum containers for compressed or liquefied gas: 1 line, 5%. A Section 232 derivative: +50%.

productGroups.label: Stranded wire and cables (not insulated)
productGroups.blurb: Aluminum stranded wire, cables and plaited bands, not electrically insulated, with or without a steel core (ACSR): 6 lines, 4.9% to 5.7%. A Section 232 derivative: +50%. Insulated cable is in Chapter 85.

productGroups.label: Household, kitchen and sanitary articles
productGroups.blurb: Aluminum cookware, bakeware, disposable foil containers, pot scourers and sanitary ware: 13 lines, 3.1% to 3.8%. Twelve are Section 232 derivatives at +25%; pot scourers (7615.10.11) are outside. Disposable aluminum containers from China are under AD/CVD orders.

productGroups.label: Other articles of aluminum
productGroups.blurb: Nails, rivets, screws and other fasteners, wire cloth, ladders, venetian blinds, luggage frames, castings, forgings and other articles: 16 lines, Free to 6%. Castings, forgings and most other articles pay +50% Section 232, ladders, blinds and luggage frames +25%, and fasteners and wire cloth (except 7616.10.90.90) are outside it.

workedExamples.title: $1 million of primary aluminum ingot from Canada, with a USMCA certification
workedExamples.body: Unwrought aluminum of 99.9% purity is **Free** under the general rate, but it is a Section 232 aluminum article, so it pays **+50% of its full value** (9903.82.02): **$500,000**. USMCA does not help, because note 16(b) collects the Section 232 duty on top of any FTA rate, and Canada's exemption ended on March 12, 2025. A 25% rate (9903.82.19) exists only for quantities Commerce authorizes for Canadian or Mexican smelters that supply U.S. vehicle makers and commit to new U.S. capacity.

workedExamples.title: Aluminum extrusions (profiles) from Canada
workedExamples.body: The base rate is **5%** (Free with a USMCA claim). Section 232 adds **50%** (9903.82.02), and since September 15, 2026 Proclamation 11065 adds the **50% Section 338 duty** (9903.03.14) on top, even for USMCA goods: **100%** with USMCA, 105% without. $200,000 of USMCA-qualifying profiles owes **$200,000**.

workedExamples.title: Aluminum billet from the United Arab Emirates
workedExamples.body: Alloy billet is **Free** at base and pays **+50%** Section 232 (9903.82.02): $50,000 on $100,000. The UAE has no FTA with the United States and no Section 232 exemption (a 2021 quota arrangement was revoked by Proclamation 10144 before it took effect). The 2026 Section 301 duty on the UAE (12.5%) does not apply to Section 232 aluminum (note 52(f)(1)).

workedExamples.title: Household aluminum foil from China
workedExamples.body: **3%** base, plus **50%** Section 232 (9903.82.02) and **25%** Section 301 (note 31, 9903.91.01): **78%**, or $78,000 on $100,000. The 12.5% 2026 Section 301 duty on China does not apply to Section 232 aluminum. Aluminum foil from China is also under antidumping and countervailing duty orders (2018, continued 2023).

workedExamples.title: Can body stock from the United Kingdom, smelted in the UK
workedExamples.body: **3%** base plus **25%** (9903.82.04) when at least 95% of the aluminum was smelted or most recently cast in the United Kingdom (note 16(d)): **28%**. Without that proof it pays the full **50%** (53% in total). UK common alloy sheet is not under an AD/CVD order.

workedExamples.title: Disposable aluminum pans from China
workedExamples.body: Household and kitchen articles are Section 232 derivatives at **25%** (9903.82.09), so this line pays its **3.1%** base plus 25%: **28.1%**. They also carry the antidumping and countervailing duty orders on disposable aluminum containers, pans, trays and lids from China (May 2025), which are company-specific and usually much higher.

workedExamples.title: Used beverage cans (scrap) from Mexico
workedExamples.body: Aluminum scrap is **Free**, is not a Section 232 article, and is on the 2026 Section 301 exemption list (9903.05.86), so Mexican scrap pays **no duty**, with or without a USMCA claim. Only Chinese scrap (25%, List 3) and Brazilian scrap (25%) pay extra. A remelt scrap ingot (7601.20.90.75), by contrast, is unwrought aluminum and pays the 50%.

notes.chapterNotes:
**Subheading note 1.** (a) *Aluminum, not alloyed*: metal containing at least 99% aluminum by weight, with iron plus silicon not over 1% and each other element (for example chromium, copper, magnesium, manganese, nickel, zinc) not over 0.1% (copper up to 0.2% if neither chromium nor manganese exceeds 0.05%). (b) *Aluminum alloys*: metallic substances in which aluminum predominates by weight over each other element, provided that at least one other element (or iron plus silicon) exceeds those limits, or the other elements together exceed 1%.

**Subheading note 2.** For subheading 7616.91, *wire* means products of any cross-sectional shape with no cross-sectional dimension over 6 mm (instead of section XV note 9(c)).

tariffUpdates.h1: HTS Chapter 76: Aluminum and Articles Thereof — Tariff Updates

seo.title: Aluminum Tariff Updates 2025–2026: 50% Section 232, Full-Value Rule, Canada, UK, Russia 200% (HTS Ch. 76) | KoalaGains
seo.shortDescription: Every U.S. aluminum tariff change with Federal Register citations: Section 232 at 25% for all countries (March 2025), 50% (June 2025), full value from April 2026, the UK's 25% rate, Canada's Section 338 duty on extrusions, the end of the IEEPA duties, and the aluminum AD/CVD orders.

tariffUpdates.intro:
This page compares two editions of the tariff schedule, the **2025 Basic Edition** (in force January 1, 2025) and the current **2026 Revision 21** (in force October 9, 2026), and lists every extra duty that reaches Chapter 76 today. Base rates did not move: the only changes are eight new statistical lines (unwrought aluminum purity grades, scrap categories and aerosol cans) at unchanged rates.

The extra duties changed a lot. In January 2025, aluminum paid 10% under Section 232, with Canada, Mexico and Australia exempt, Argentina under a quota and the EU and UK under tariff-rate quotas. Proclamation 10895 ended those arrangements and raised the rate to **25% on March 12, 2025**; Proclamation 10947 raised it to **50% on June 4, 2025** (UK stayed at 25%); and Proclamation 11021 rebuilt the program on **April 6, 2026** as headings 9903.82.02 (50%) and 9903.82.09 (25% for household and some other derivatives), charged on the **full customs value**. Russian aluminum has paid **200%** since March 10, 2023. Canadian extrusions and tubes pay a further **50% under Section 338** since September 15, 2026. The IEEPA duties ended on **February 24, 2026** and never added to Section 232 aluminum after June 4, 2025; the Section 122 surcharge and the 2026 Section 301 duties leave it alone too. China's Section 301 duty (25%) does stack.

Antidumping and countervailing duty orders cover extrusions, sheet, foil and disposable containers. They are company-specific, listed below for reference, and **not included in the tariff calculator**.
tariffUpdates.scope: Chapter 99 measures that reach Chapter 76 from any country: Section 232 aluminum (note 16) and the 200% on Russian aluminum (note 19), China Section 301 (notes 20, 31), the 2026 Section 301 actions on 60 economies and Brazil (notes 50, 52), Canada Section 338 (note 51), Russia's rates in lieu of column 2 (note 30), the civil aircraft reliefs (notes 2, 35, 51(d), 52(d)), the scheduled Nicaragua Section 301 duty (note 29), and the ended IEEPA and Section 122 duties. The aluminum antidumping and countervailing duty orders are listed for reference; the calculator does not model them. For the rate each supplier pays, see Rates by country.

It does charge scrap, powders, tanks, pot scourers, fasteners and wire cloth. Civil aircraft articles are relieved (9903.05.05). Brazilian common alloy sheet and foil are also under AD orders.

changes.title: No Chapter 76 base-rate changes
changes.detail: 116 of 124 Chapter 76 lines carry the same General, Special and Column 2 rates in the 2026 Revision 21 as in the 2025 Basic Edition. The other eight are new statistical lines at unchanged rates: 7601.10.60.30 was split into 7601.10.60.40 (99.9% aluminum or greater) and 7601.10.60.45; the scrap lines 7602.00.00.95–.98 became 7602.00.00.45 (wheels), .55 (industrial), .65 and .75; and 7612.90.10.30 was split into 7612.90.10.40 (aerosol cans) and 7612.90.10.45.

changes.title: Five-year reviews of the 2021 aluminum foil orders begin
changes.detail: The ITC and Commerce instituted five-year (sunset) reviews of the antidumping duty orders on aluminum foil from Armenia, Brazil, Oman, Russia and Türkiye and the countervailing duty orders on Oman and Türkiye. The orders stay in force during the reviews.

changes.title: Section 338 duty on Canadian aluminum extrusions and tubes, on top of Section 232
changes.detail: Proclamation 11065 added aluminum bars, rods and profiles (7604) and tubes and pipes (7608) to the products of Canada that pay the 50% Section 338 duty (9903.03.14, note 51(b)(3)), and made the duty apply in addition to Section 232. It is charged even on USMCA goods. Canadian extrusions and tubes now pay 100% or more; other Canadian aluminum stays at 50%. Civil aircraft articles are relieved (9903.03.16).

changes.title: 2026 Section 301 tariffs on 60 economies: Section 232 aluminum exempt
changes.detail: The 10% or 12.5% duties on goods of 60 economies (9903.05.20–9903.05.84) took effect. They do not apply to Section 232 aluminum (note 52(f)(1)), and scrap is on the general exemption list (note 52(b)). In Chapter 76 they charge 12 lines: powders, tanks, pot scourers, fasteners and wire cloth. USMCA goods are exempt.

changes.title: Section 122 surcharge expired
changes.detail: The 10% surcharge on products of all countries (9903.03.01) expired at the close of July 23, 2026. It never applied to Section 232 aluminum (Proclamation 11012; note 2(aa)), so in Chapter 76 it reached only scrap, powders, tanks, pot scourers, fasteners and wire cloth.

changes.title: Section 301 tariff on Brazil: Section 232 aluminum exempt, scrap not
changes.detail: The 25% duty on goods of Brazil (9903.05.01) took effect. Section 232 aluminum is excluded (note 50(a)(vi)(1)), so it reaches only the 17 non-Section 232 lines, including aluminum scrap.

changes.title: Proclamation 11045: half-rate imports for companies building U.S. primary aluminum capacity
changes.detail: Proclamation 11045 told Commerce to set up a program under which companies with an approved plan to build, expand or refurbish a U.S. primary aluminum smelter (construction to start by January 20, 2029) may import primary aluminum, up to the plant's expected annual output, at half the Section 232 rate. As of the 2026 Revision 21 no HTS heading for it exists, and Commerce has not yet published procedures in the Federal Register.
changes.now: Half the Section 232 rate (approved plans only)

changes.title: Full sunset reviews of the 2021 common alloy aluminum sheet orders
changes.detail: The ITC decided to conduct full five-year reviews of the antidumping duty orders on common alloy aluminum sheet from Bahrain, Brazil, Croatia, Egypt, Germany, India, Indonesia, Italy, Oman, Romania, Serbia, Slovenia, South Africa, Spain, Taiwan and Türkiye and the countervailing duty orders on Bahrain, India and Türkiye. The orders stay in force during the reviews.

changes.title: Proclamation 11032 adjusts the metals program
changes.detail: From June 8, 2026 a derivative counts as made from U.S. aluminum when at least 85% of its aluminum content was smelted and cast in the United States (10%, 9903.82.06), and new rates apply to industrial and mobile equipment derivatives outside Chapter 76. Chapter 76 rates stay at 50% and 25% (UK 25% and 15%).

changes.title: Commerce corrects the Section 232 annex
changes.detail: Commerce added heading 9903.82.01 (articles on the note 16 lists that contain no aluminum, steel or copper pay no Section 232 duty) from April 6, 2026, and made other technical corrections to the HTS annex.

changes.title: Commerce opens the 25% route for Canadian and Mexican aluminum producers
changes.detail: Commerce set out how aluminum and steel producers with plants in Canada or Mexico that supply U.S. vehicle makers can apply for a tariff reduction of up to half (not below 25%), limited to quantities matched to newly committed U.S. production. Approved aluminum articles enter under 9903.82.19 (+25%) if they qualify for USMCA and were smelted and cast in Canada or Mexico.

changes.title: Section 232 metals program rebuilt on full value (Proclamation 11021)
changes.detail: Proclamation 11021 replaced the aluminum headings of note 19 (9903.85.02–9903.85.15) with 9903.82.02–9903.82.26, charged on the full customs value regardless of metal content (before, Chapter 76 derivatives paid on the aluminum content). Aluminum articles and the (c)(ii) derivatives stay at 50% (9903.82.02); household articles, ladders, blinds and luggage frames drop to 25% (9903.82.09); the UK needs at least 95% UK-smelted or cast aluminum for 25% (9903.82.04) or 15% (9903.82.05). Russian aluminum stays at 200%. Manufacturing drawback is allowed only for the 25% derivatives of trade-agreement partners; goods entering a foreign-trade zone must take privileged foreign status; the derivatives inclusions process ended.

changes.title: Section 122 surcharge replaces the IEEPA tariffs; Section 232 aluminum outside it
changes.detail: A 10% surcharge on products of all countries (9903.03.01) applied until July 23, 2026. Proclamation 11012 says it does not apply to goods subject to Section 232, so aluminum paid only the 50%; scrap, powders, tanks, pot scourers, fasteners and wire cloth paid the 10% unless USMCA was claimed.

changes.title: All IEEPA tariffs end
changes.detail: After the Supreme Court held on February 20, 2026 (Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump) that IEEPA does not authorize tariffs, Executive Order 14389 ended the Canada, Mexico, China and reciprocal duties, and CBP stopped collecting them from 12:00 a.m. ET on February 24, 2026. Section 232 aluminum duties are not IEEPA duties and continued unchanged. For Chapter 76 the IEEPA duties had mattered mainly for scrap, powders, fasteners and the other non-Section 232 lines.

changes.title: Section 301 tariff on Nicaragua phases in from 2027
changes.detail: Products of Nicaragua that are not CAFTA-DR originating goods will pay +10% from January 1, 2027 and +15% from January 1, 2028 (9903.89.01, U.S. note 29). Note 29 has no Section 232 carve-out, so it will add to the 50% on Nicaraguan aluminum. The rate is 0% in 2026.

changes.title: Authority to halve Section 232 for some Canadian and Mexican aluminum
changes.detail: Proclamation 10984 (medium- and heavy-duty vehicles) authorized Commerce to cut the Section 232 aluminum and steel duty by up to half, but not below 25%, for limited quantities from Canadian or Mexican producers that supply U.S. vehicle makers and commit to new U.S. capacity. The aluminum must qualify for USMCA and be smelted and cast in Canada or Mexico (heading 9903.82.19).

changes.title: UK Economic Prosperity Deal: UK aluminum stays at 25%
changes.detail: Executive Order 14309, implementing the U.S.-UK Economic Prosperity Deal, directed Commerce to design a tariff-rate quota for UK aluminum articles and derivatives at a time it deems appropriate; the deal's general terms speak of a quota at most-favored-nation rates once the UK meets U.S. supply-chain and ownership requirements. No quota has been established. UK aluminum stays at 25% under Proclamation 10947; since April 6, 2026 that rate requires at least 95% UK-smelted or most recently cast aluminum.

changes.title: Section 232 aluminum tariff doubled to 50%
changes.detail: Proclamation 10947 raised the Section 232 aluminum and steel duties from 25% to 50% for goods entered from 12:01 a.m. EDT on June 4, 2025, except for the UK (25%). It also amended Executive Order 14289 so that aluminum subject to Section 232 no longer paid the Canada and Mexico IEEPA duties.

changes.title: AD/CVD orders on disposable aluminum containers from China
changes.detail: Commerce issued antidumping and countervailing duty orders on disposable aluminum containers, pans, trays and lids from China (mainly 7615.10.71.25; also 7612.90, 7615.10 and 8309.90 for lids).

changes.title: Non-stacking order between IEEPA and Section 232
changes.detail: Executive Order 14289, retroactive to March 4, 2025, set an order of precedence so that Canadian and Mexican goods did not pay both the IEEPA duties and Section 232. Proclamation 10947 settled it from June 4, 2025: Section 232 aluminum no longer paid the IEEPA duties.

changes.title: Reciprocal tariff excludes Section 232 aluminum
changes.detail: Executive Order 14257 set the reciprocal tariffs from April 5, 2025 but excluded aluminum articles and derivatives subject to Section 232. Non-Section 232 Chapter 76 lines paid it. Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Aluminum exemptions and quotas end; rate raised to 25%; more derivatives
changes.detail: Proclamation 10895 ended the arrangements with Argentina, Australia, Canada, Mexico, the EU and the UK, raised the Section 232 aluminum duty from 10% to 25%, and extended it to more derivative aluminum articles (U.S. note 19(j): structures, cans and containers, household articles and other articles of Chapter 76). The 200% on Russian aluminum continued.
changes.before: +10%, many countries exempt or under quotas
changes.countries: Argentina, Australia, Canada, Mexico, EU, UK

changes.title: IEEPA duties on Canada and Mexico
changes.detail: +25% on goods of Canada (9903.01.10) and Mexico (9903.01.01) from March 4, 2025; USMCA goods were exempted from March 7, 2025. Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: No new AD/CVD orders on aluminum extrusions from 14 countries
changes.detail: Commerce had found dumping or subsidies on aluminum extrusions from China, Colombia, Ecuador, India, Indonesia, Italy, Malaysia, Mexico, South Korea, Taiwan, Thailand, Türkiye, the UAE and Vietnam, but the ITC determined that the U.S. industry was not materially injured or threatened, so no orders were issued. The 2011 orders on extrusions from China remain.

changes.title: China Section 301: aluminum products to 25%
changes.detail: After its four-year review, USTR moved Chinese steel and aluminum products to U.S. note 31 (9903.91.01) at 25%, including unwrought aluminum, extrusions, wire, sheet, foil and tubes, from September 27, 2024.

changes.title: Common alloy aluminum sheet orders on China continued
changes.detail: After five-year reviews, Commerce continued the 2019 antidumping and countervailing duty orders on common alloy aluminum sheet from China.

changes.title: Mexico: duty on aluminum smelted or cast in China, Russia, Belarus or Iran
changes.detail: Proclamation 10782 charged the then-10% Section 232 duty on Mexican aluminum whose primary or secondary country of smelt or country of most recent cast was China, Russia, Belarus or Iran, and required smelt and cast information. Superseded on March 12, 2025, when all Mexican aluminum became dutiable.

changes.title: Chinese foil orders reach foil finished in Korea and Thailand
changes.detail: Commerce found that aluminum foil completed in Korea and Thailand from Chinese-origin foil circumvents the orders on China, so such foil can owe the China AD/CVD cash deposits.

changes.title: Aluminum foil orders on China continued
changes.detail: After five-year reviews, Commerce continued the 2018 antidumping and countervailing duty orders on aluminum foil from China.

changes.title: Common alloy sheet orders reach 4017 aluminum sheet from China
changes.detail: Commerce found that imports of 4017 aluminum sheet from China circumvent the common alloy aluminum sheet orders, which therefore cover it.

changes.title: Russia: 70% in lieu of column 2 on aluminum
changes.detail: Proclamation 10523 raised the rate on Russian aluminum and other metals of note 30(d) to 70% in place of the column 2 rate (Russia has paid column 2 rates since April 9, 2022). It applies to 54 Chapter 76 lines, on top of which the 200% Section 232 duty is charged.

changes.title: 200% Section 232 duty on Russian aluminum
changes.detail: Proclamation 10522 set a 200% duty on aluminum articles and derivatives that are products of Russia from March 10, 2023, and on those of any origin containing primary aluminum smelted in Russia or cast in Russia from April 10, 2023.

changes.title: UK aluminum tariff-rate quota
changes.detail: Proclamation 10405 let UK aluminum enter free of Section 232 duty within an annual quota, with 10% above it, from June 1, 2022. Ended March 12, 2025.

changes.title: EU aluminum tariff-rate quota
changes.detail: Proclamation 10327 set a duty-free quota for EU aluminum from January 1, 2022; Proclamation 10690 extended it and required a certificate of analysis from January 1, 2024. Ended March 12, 2025.

changes.title: AD/CVD orders on aluminum foil from five countries
changes.detail: Commerce issued antidumping duty orders on aluminum foil from Armenia, Brazil, Oman, Russia and Türkiye and countervailing duty orders on Oman and Türkiye.

changes.title: Aluminum import licenses (AIM) required
changes.detail: Commerce's Aluminum Import Monitoring and Analysis system (19 CFR part 361) requires an import license, with the countries of smelt and cast, for every formal entry of unwrought aluminum, extrusions, wire, sheet, foil, tubes, fittings, castings and forgings. Compliance began June 28, 2021; from June 29, 2022 filers can no longer answer "unknown" for the smelt fields.

changes.title: AD/CVD orders on common alloy aluminum sheet from 16 countries
changes.detail: Commerce issued antidumping duty orders on common alloy aluminum sheet from Bahrain, Brazil, Croatia, Egypt, Germany, India, Indonesia, Italy, Oman, Romania, Serbia, Slovenia, South Africa, Spain, Taiwan and Türkiye, and countervailing duty orders on Bahrain, India and Türkiye.

changes.title: UAE aluminum quota arrangement revoked before it took effect
changes.detail: Proclamation 10139 (January 19, 2021) would have exempted UAE aluminum from Section 232 under a quota from February 3, 2021; Proclamation 10144 terminated it before it took effect, so UAE aluminum kept paying the duty.

changes.title: 10% briefly reimposed on Canadian non-alloyed unwrought aluminum
changes.detail: Proclamation 10060 reimposed the 10% duty on non-alloyed unwrought aluminum (7601.10) from Canada from August 16, 2020; Proclamation 10106 removed it retroactively from September 1, 2020.

changes.title: First Section 232 aluminum derivatives
changes.detail: Proclamation 9980 extended the 10% aluminum duty to certain derivatives, including aluminum stranded wire and cable (7614) and some vehicle stampings, from February 8, 2020.

changes.title: Canada and Mexico exempted from Section 232 aluminum
changes.detail: Proclamation 9893 removed the Section 232 aluminum duty on Canada and Mexico from May 20, 2019. The exemption lasted until March 12, 2025.

changes.title: AD/CVD orders on common alloy aluminum sheet from China
changes.detail: Commerce issued antidumping and countervailing duty orders on common alloy aluminum sheet from China.

changes.title: Section 232 aluminum extended to the EU, Canada and Mexico
changes.detail: Proclamation 9758 ended the temporary exemptions of the EU, Canada and Mexico on June 1, 2018, set a quota for Argentina and kept Australia exempt.

changes.title: AD/CVD orders on aluminum foil from China
changes.detail: Commerce issued antidumping and countervailing duty orders on certain aluminum foil from China.

changes.title: Section 232 aluminum tariff begins at 10%
changes.detail: Proclamation 9704 imposed a 10% duty on aluminum articles (unwrought aluminum, extrusions, wire, sheet, foil, tubes, fittings, castings and forgings) from March 23, 2018, with temporary exemptions for some countries.

changes.title: AD/CVD orders on aluminum extrusions from China
changes.detail: Commerce issued antidumping and countervailing duty orders on aluminum extrusions from China (mainly 7604 and 7608, and extrusions forming parts of other articles); they were continued in 2017 and 2022.

understandIndustry.why:
U.S. imports of Chapter 76 aluminum and aluminum articles were **$26.47B in 2025**, -6.5% from $28.31B in 2024 (peak: $36.66B in 2022). The five largest suppliers were Canada ($9.69B), China ($1.97B), Mexico ($1.81B), the UAE ($1.61B), South Korea ($1.23B); Canada alone shipped $9.69B (37% of the total). By product group the largest were unwrought aluminum (7601, $9.94B), plates, sheets and strip (7606, $3.83B), structures, doors, windows and frames (7610, $2.24B). Scrap (7602), outside Section 232 and Free for most suppliers, was $2.16B.

2025 was also the year Section 232 changed most: every country exemption and quota ended on March 12, the rate rose from 10% to 25% the same day and to 50% on June 4, so suppliers that had shipped duty-free, such as Canada, Mexico and Australia, or within quotas, such as the EU and UK, paid the full duty. China, whose aluminum pays 75% plus AD/CVD on extrusions, sheet, foil and containers, shipped $1.97B. 

2025 is the latest full year of U.S. trade data. Duty-collected figures aren't available from an official source yet.

industryAreas.intro:
Each cell is the base rate for that product group plus the extra duties for that country, minus any preference, from the current tariff schedule. For aluminum articles and most derivatives the answer is almost the same everywhere: **50%**, because Section 232 has no country exemptions and is collected on top of FTA and USMCA rates; household articles pay **25%**. Canada pays **100%** on extrusions and tubes (Section 338 adds 50%), China **75%** (Section 301 adds 25%), Russia **over 250%** (200% plus 70% in place of column 2), and the UK **25%** when the aluminum was smelted or most recently cast in the UK (the cells show the 50% default).

The non-Section 232 groups differ: scrap is Free except for China and Brazil, and powders, tanks, pot scourers, fasteners and wire cloth pay their base rate plus, for most countries, the 2026 Section 301 duty (10% or 12.5%). The table does **not** include antidumping or countervailing duties, which apply company by company to extrusions, sheet, foil and disposable containers from the countries named in Tariff updates.

seo.shortDescription: The rules for each HTS Chapter 76 aluminum line: Commerce AIM aluminum import license, country of smelt and cast, Section 232 entry (9903.82.02 / 9903.82.09), FTZ status, marking, AD/CVD scope, plus the legal ways to pay less: UK-smelted aluminum, U.S.-smelted derivatives, the Canada/Mexico 25% route, civil aircraft relief, classification and drawback.

tariffEngineering.intro:
For aluminum, the paperwork is part of the duty. Every formal entry of unwrought aluminum, extrusions, wire, sheet, foil, tubes, fittings, castings and forgings needs a **Commerce aluminum import license (AIM)**, and every Section 232 aluminum entry must report the **countries where the primary aluminum was smelted and where it was most recently cast**. The Section 232 heading (9903.82.02 or 9903.82.09, or a lower-rate heading) is reported next to the Chapter 76 line, and the duty is charged on the full value with no FTA reduction.

The legal ways to pay less are narrow: country exemptions, quotas and product exclusions are gone, and drawback of Section 232 duty is limited. What remains: UK-smelted aluminum (25%), derivatives made from U.S.-smelted aluminum (10%), Commerce-authorized Canadian or Mexican quantities (25%), civil aircraft relief for tubes, avoiding Chinese origin and Canadian extrusions, classifying correctly, and checking AD/CVD scope before you buy. Each rule and lever links to its regulation or proclamation.

levers.title: Buy UK aluminum smelted or cast in the UK
levers.saves: Half the Section 232 duty: 25% (9903.82.04) instead of 50%, or 15% (9903.82.05) instead of 25% on household articles
levers.appliesTo: Section 232 aluminum lines of the United Kingdom
levers.document: A certificate of analysis or mill records showing the countries of smelt and cast, reported in ACE; at least 95% of the aluminum must have been smelted or most recently cast in the UK.
levers.caveat: Origin must be the UK and the 95% test must be met; otherwise 50% (25%). The quota contemplated by Executive Order 14309 has not been set up.

citations.label: HTSUS Ch. 99, subch. III, U.S. note 16(d), headings 9903.82.04–9903.82.05

levers.title: Derivatives made from U.S.-smelted aluminum
levers.saves: 40 or 15 points: 10% (9903.82.06) instead of 50% or 25% on derivative articles
levers.appliesTo: Chapter 76 derivatives (7610, 7612–7615, 7616.10.90.90, 7616.99) whose aluminum content is at least 85% smelted and cast in the United States
levers.document: Smelt and cast records for the aluminum content (by weight), kept for CBP; report 9903.82.06.
levers.caveat: Not for the aluminum articles of note 16(c)(i) (ingot, extrusions, sheet, foil, tubes, castings and forgings), and not for Russia. The 85% threshold applies from June 8, 2026 (Proclamation 11032).

citations.label: HTSUS Ch. 99, subch. III, U.S. note 16(e), heading 9903.82.06

levers.title: Canada or Mexico: the Commerce-authorized 25% rate
levers.saves: Half the Section 232 duty (25% instead of 50%) on authorized quantities
levers.appliesTo: Aluminum articles (note 16(c)(i)) of Canada or Mexico that qualify for USMCA and were smelted and cast in Canada or Mexico
levers.document: Commerce authorization for the producer (submission under the April 23, 2026 procedures), USMCA certification of origin, and entry under heading 9903.82.19.
levers.caveat: Only for producers that supply U.S. automobile or heavy-vehicle makers and commit to new U.S. aluminum capacity; limited to the quantity Commerce sets. Canadian extrusions and tubes still pay the 50% Section 338 duty.

citations.label: HTSUS Ch. 99, subch. III, U.S. note 16(i), heading 9903.82.19

levers.title: Civil aircraft tubes and pipes
levers.saves: The Section 232 duty (UK, Japan, EU, Korea), the Canada Section 338 duty and the 2026 Section 301 duty on qualifying civil aircraft articles
levers.appliesTo: Aluminum tubes and pipes (7608) for civil aircraft that meet general note 6
levers.document: Civil aircraft certification under general note 6 and 19 CFR 10.183; report the relief heading (9903.96.01 UK, 9903.96.02 Japan, 9903.02.76 EU, 9903.02.81 Korea, 9903.03.16 Canada, 9903.05.88).
levers.caveat: Only goods of the countries named, only on the listed provisions, and only for civil (not military or unmanned) aircraft.

citations.label: HTSUS Ch. 99, subch. III, U.S. notes 2(v), 35, 51(d), 52(d)

levers.title: Avoid Chinese origin and Russian metal
levers.saves: 25% of value on Chinese aluminum (Section 301 on top of Section 232), and the 200% that any aluminum smelted or cast in Russia owes
levers.document: Mill certificates and the certificate of analysis showing where the aluminum was smelted and cast and where the product was made. For the tariff, origin follows the last substantial transformation under 19 CFR 102.20; ask CBP for a binding ruling.
levers.caveat: Third-country processing does not change the Section 232 rate (50% everywhere) and can fall under AD/CVD circumvention findings: Chinese foil finished in Korea or Thailand owes the China foil deposits. Canadian extrusions and tubes pay 50% more than other Canadian aluminum.

citations.label: HTSUS Ch. 99, subch. III, U.S. notes 19(m), 31

levers.title: Classify scrap, fasteners and derivatives correctly
levers.saves: The 50% or 25% Section 232 duty on lines that are not on the note 16(c) lists: scrap (7602), powders (7603), tanks (7611), pot scourers (7615.10.11), fasteners (7616.10, except 7616.10.90.90) and wire cloth (7616.91)
levers.document: Technical specifications (scrap grade vs remelt scrap ingot; fastener type) and, if unsure, a CBP binding ruling.
levers.caveat: Classification follows the product, not the duty: a remelt scrap ingot (7601.20.90.75) is unwrought aluminum at 50%. Most non-232 lines still pay the 2026 Section 301 duty.

citations.label: HTSUS Ch. 99, subch. III, U.S. note 16(c)

levers.title: Claim USMCA for the non-232 lines
levers.saves: The 10% Section 301 duty on Canadian and Mexican powders, tanks, pot scourers, fasteners and wire cloth (9903.05.93, 9903.05.94), plus their base rate
levers.appliesTo: The 12 Chapter 76 lines that pay the 2026 Section 301 duty, for originating goods of Canada or Mexico
levers.document: A USMCA certification of origin from the importer, exporter or producer (no set format), available to CBP on request.
levers.caveat: A USMCA claim does not reduce Section 232 (note 16(b)) or the Section 338 duty on Canadian extrusions and tubes.

citations.label: HTSUS Ch. 99, subch. III, U.S. note 52(g)–(h)

levers.title: Check AD/CVD scope before you buy
levers.saves: The whole antidumping or countervailing duty, when the product or producer is outside the order
levers.appliesTo: Extrusions (China), common alloy sheet (China and 16 countries), foil (China, Armenia, Brazil, Oman, Russia, Türkiye) and disposable containers (China)
levers.document: The order's written scope (it, not the HTS number, decides) and the producer's company-specific cash-deposit rate; when unsure, request a scope ruling from Commerce.
levers.caveat: A product in scope pays the cash deposit even if entered under another HTS line; the China extrusions orders also reach extrusions that are parts of other goods. AD/CVD rates change with each administrative review.

levers.title: Drawback: limited for Section 232
levers.saves: Up to 99% of the base rate, Section 301 and other ordinary duties on goods that are exported or used in exported products; Section 232 only as below
levers.appliesTo: All lines; Section 232 duty only on the 25% derivatives (Annex I-B) of trade-agreement partners
levers.document: A drawback claim to CBP with import and export records (19 CFR part 191).
levers.caveat: Proclamation 11021 allows manufacturing drawback of Section 232 duty only for Annex I-B and III derivatives of the UK, EU, Japan, Korea, Mexico, Canada and later agreement partners, made from partner-smelted aluminum, and not of a type under an AD/CVD order (disposable containers are). The 50% aluminum articles get none. AD/CVD are never refundable (19 CFR 191.3).

rules.title: Aluminum import license (AIM) before filing the entry summary, with the countries of smelt and most recent cast; for 7601, 7604–7609 and 7616.99.51.60/.70, consumption and FTZ entries, not for informal entries
Report the primary and secondary country of smelt and the country of most recent cast on every Section 232 aluminum entry (ACE)

Section 232: report 9903.82.02 (50%) or 9903.82.09 (25%), or 9903.82.04 / .05 (UK), .06 (U.S.-smelted), .19 (authorized Canada/Mexico), 9903.85.67 / .68 (Russia) with the Chapter 76 line; duty on the full value, on top of any FTA rate

citations.label: HTSUS Ch. 99, subch. III, U.S. note 16

rules.title: Section 232 aluminum admitted to a foreign-trade zone must take privileged foreign status (duty fixed at admission)
Country of origin marking on the article or its container
Russian aluminum, or aluminum of any origin smelted or cast in Russia: 200% (9903.85.67 / .68); Russian goods also pay column 2 or 70% in lieu of column 2 on note 30(d) lines

citations.label: HTSUS Ch. 99, subch. III, U.S. notes 19(m), 30

rules.title: Aluminum extrusions AD/CVD orders on China (2011, continued 2022), including extrusions that are parts of other goods; the 2024 case on 14 other countries ended without orders. Not in the tariff calculator

Common alloy aluminum sheet AD/CVD orders: China (2019, continued 2024; includes 4017 sheet) and Bahrain, Brazil, Croatia, Egypt, Germany, India, Indonesia, Italy, Oman, Romania, Serbia, Slovenia, South Africa, Spain, Taiwan, Türkiye (2021, CVD on Bahrain, India, Türkiye; in sunset review). Not in the tariff calculator

Aluminum foil AD/CVD orders: China (2018, continued 2023; foil finished in Korea and Thailand from Chinese foil covered) and Armenia, Brazil, Oman, Russia, Türkiye (2021, CVD on Oman and Türkiye; sunset review begun October 2026). Not in the tariff calculator
Disposable aluminum containers, pans, trays and lids AD/CVD orders on China (May 2025). Not in the tariff calculator

groups.label: Unwrought aluminum (ingot, billet, slab)
groups.note: Section 232 aluminum article: AIM license, smelt and cast reporting, 50%. Canadian and Mexican smelters can get Commerce-authorized 25% quantities.

groups.label: Aluminum waste and scrap
groups.note: Outside Section 232 and AIM; on the 2026 Section 301 exemption list. Free except for China (25%), Brazil (25%) and Russia (column 2). Remelt scrap ingot is 7601, not scrap.

groups.label: Aluminum powders and flakes
groups.note: Outside Section 232 and AIM; pays the 2026 Section 301 duty for most countries.

groups.label: Bars, rods and profiles (extrusions)
groups.note: Extrusions: AIM license, smelt and cast reporting, 50%; Canada also 50% Section 338. AD/CVD orders on extrusions from China.

groups.label: Aluminum wire
groups.note: Section 232 aluminum article: AIM license, smelt and cast reporting, 50%.

groups.label: Plates, sheets and strip (over 0.2 mm)
groups.note: Sheet and plate: AIM license, 50%; common alloy sheet AD/CVD orders on China and 16 other countries.

groups.label: Aluminum foil (0.2 mm or less)
groups.note: Foil: AIM license, 50%; foil AD/CVD orders on China (and Chinese foil finished in Korea or Thailand), Armenia, Brazil, Oman, Russia and Türkiye. Some foil-gauge can stock is in the sheet orders.

groups.label: Tubes and pipes
groups.note: Tubes and pipes: AIM license, 50%; Canada also 50% Section 338; civil aircraft relief for some countries. Extruded tubes from China can fall within the extrusions orders.

groups.label: Tube or pipe fittings
groups.note: Section 232 aluminum article: AIM license, smelt and cast reporting, 50%.

groups.label: Structures, doors, windows and frames
groups.note: Section 232 derivative at 50% (10% with U.S.-smelted aluminum). Window and door frames made of Chinese extrusions can fall within the extrusions orders.

groups.label: Reservoirs and tanks (over 300 l)
groups.note: Outside Section 232; pays the 2026 Section 301 duty for most countries.

groups.label: Casks, drums, cans and boxes (up to 300 l)
groups.note: Section 232 derivative at 50%. Disposable container lids of 7612.90 can fall within the China containers orders.

groups.label: Containers for compressed or liquefied gas
Stranded wire and cables (not insulated)
groups.note: Section 232 derivative at 50%. Insulated aluminum wire and cable is in Chapter 85 (the China aluminum wire and cable orders cover 8544, not 7614).

groups.label: Household, kitchen and sanitary articles
groups.note: Household articles: Section 232 derivative at 25% (UK 15%, U.S.-smelted 10%); pot scourers outside. Disposable aluminum containers from China are under AD/CVD orders.

groups.label: Other articles of aluminum
groups.note: Castings and forgings (7616.99.51.60/.70) need the AIM license and pay 50%; ladders, blinds and luggage frames pay 25%; most fasteners and wire cloth are outside Section 232.

seo.shortDescription: Answers to what people search about U.S. aluminum tariffs: the current rate, whether the 50% aluminum tariff is still in effect, aluminum tariffs on Canada, Mexico, China, the UK and EU, derivatives, smelt and cast, the AIM import license, extrusions, foil and HS codes.
keywords: are aluminum tariffs still in effect
what is the tariff on aluminum

finalConclusion.intro: Straight answers to the most-searched questions about U.S. tariffs on aluminum imports, by country, by product and by HS code. Each answer links to the page with the detail and the official sources.
keyTakeaways: Aluminum articles and most derivatives (HTS 7601, 7604–7614, much of 7616) pay the Section 232 duty of 50% of their full customs value, from every country and on top of any FTA or USMCA rate; household articles, ladders, blinds and luggage frames pay 25%. UK aluminum smelted or cast in the UK pays 25% (15%).

Chinese aluminum pays 75% (50% Section 232 + 25% Section 301), Russian aluminum 200% more (also when smelted or cast in Russia and shipped from elsewhere), and Canadian extrusions and tubes 100% since September 15, 2026 (Section 338). Scrap, powders, tanks and most fasteners are outside Section 232.

The IEEPA tariffs ended February 24, 2026 and the Section 122 surcharge July 23, 2026; neither added to Section 232 aluminum. Antidumping and countervailing duties on extrusions, sheet, foil and disposable containers come on top and are not in the calculator.
In 2025 the U.S. imported $26.47B of Chapter 76 products, Canada ($9.69B) and China ($1.97B) first.

faqs.question: What is the current U.S. tariff on aluminum?
searchedAs: what is the tariff on aluminum
how much is the tariff on aluminum
what is the current tariff on aluminum
faqs.answer: 50% of the full customs value for aluminum articles (unwrought aluminum, extrusions, wire, sheet, foil, tubes, castings) and most derivatives, from every country, under Section 232 heading 9903.82.02, on top of the base rate (Free to 6.5%). Household articles, ladders, blinds and luggage frames pay 25% (9903.82.09). UK aluminum smelted or most recently cast in the UK pays 25% (9903.82.04). Chinese aluminum pays another 25% under Section 301, Russian aluminum 200%, and Canadian extrusions and tubes another 50% under Section 338.

faqs.question: Is the 50% aluminum tariff still in effect, and when did it start?
searchedAs: are aluminum tariffs still in effect
is there still a tariff on aluminum
is there a 50 tariff on aluminum
are steel and aluminum tariffs still in effect
faqs.answer: Yes. Proclamation 10947 raised the Section 232 aluminum duty from 25% to 50% for goods entered from 12:01 a.m. EDT on June 4, 2025. Proclamation 11021 kept 50% when it moved the duty to heading 9903.82.02 on the full customs value from April 6, 2026, and it is in the current tariff schedule (2026 Revision 21). The Supreme Court's February 20, 2026 ruling in Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump ended only the IEEPA tariffs; the aluminum tariff rests on Section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act of 1962 and was not affected.

faqs.question: What is the tariff on aluminum from Canada?
searchedAs: what is the tariff on aluminum from canada
is there a tariff on aluminum from canada
faqs.answer: 50% on Canadian aluminum articles and most derivatives, with or without a USMCA claim: Canada's Section 232 exemption ended March 12, 2025, and note 16(b) collects the duty on top of the USMCA rate. Since September 15, 2026 Canadian extrusions (7604) and tubes and pipes (7608) also pay the 50% Section 338 duty (Proclamation 11065), so 100% in total. Commerce can authorize limited quantities at 25% (9903.82.19) for Canadian smelters that supply U.S. vehicle makers and commit to new U.S. capacity. Canadian scrap stays Free. Canada shipped $9.69B of Chapter 76 goods in 2025.

faqs.question: What is the tariff on aluminum from Mexico?
searchedAs: what is the tariff on aluminum from mexico
faqs.answer: 50% on Mexican aluminum articles and most derivatives (Section 232, 9903.82.02), 25% on household articles, even with a USMCA certification. Mexico's exemption, and the 2024 rule that charged duty on Mexican aluminum smelted or cast in China, Russia, Belarus or Iran, ended on March 12, 2025, when all Mexican aluminum became dutiable. A 25% rate is possible only for Commerce-authorized quantities (9903.82.19). Mexico shipped $1.81B in 2025.

faqs.question: What is the tariff on aluminum from China?
searchedAs: aluminum tariff from china to usa
is there a tariff on aluminum from china
faqs.answer: 75% to 81.5% on Chinese aluminum articles: 50% Section 232 plus 25% Section 301 (U.S. note 31, heading 9903.91.01, since September 27, 2024) plus the base rate; a few foil, door and window lines pay 7.5% under List 4A instead. Chinese scrap pays 25%. Chinese aluminum extrusions, common alloy sheet, foil and disposable containers also carry antidumping and countervailing duties, company by company.

faqs.question: Where does the U.S. import aluminum from?
faqs.answer: In 2025 the United States imported $26.47B of Chapter 76 aluminum and aluminum articles. The largest suppliers were Canada ($9.69B), China ($1.97B), Mexico ($1.81B), the UAE ($1.61B), South Korea ($1.23B). The biggest product groups were unwrought aluminum (7601, $9.94B), plates, sheets and strip (7606, $3.83B), structures, doors, windows and frames (7610, $2.24B). Aluminum articles from all of them pay the 50% Section 232 duty today (UK 25% with UK-smelted aluminum, China 75%, Canadian extrusions and tubes 100%).

faqs.question: What are aluminum tariffs by country, including the UK, EU and Japan?
searchedAs: steel and aluminum tariffs by country
what is the tariff on aluminum from japan
faqs.answer: For aluminum articles: 50% for Canada (100% on extrusions and tubes), Mexico, the UAE, Bahrain, India, Korea, Japan, the EU and every other country; 25% for UK aluminum smelted or most recently cast in the UK; 75% for China; 200% more for Russia. The EU and UK quotas and the Japan and Korea trade deals did not change the Section 232 aluminum rate (only civil aircraft parts are relieved). Differences between countries show up on scrap and fasteners, and in AD/CVD duties.

faqs.question: Which aluminum derivatives are covered by Section 232?
faqs.answer: The lists are in U.S. note 16(c) to Chapter 99. In Chapter 76: aluminum articles (7601, 7604–7609, castings and forgings 7616.99.51.60/.70) and the derivatives in 7610, 7612–7614, 7616.10.90.90 and the other 7616.99.51 lines pay 50%; household articles (7615), luggage frames, ladders and blinds pay 25%. Outside Chapter 76, hundreds of derivative products of other chapters are listed and pay only when aluminum is at least 15% of their weight. Scrap, powders, tanks, pot scourers, most fasteners and wire cloth are not covered.

faqs.question: How are aluminum tariffs calculated?
searchedAs: how are steel and aluminum tariffs calculated
faqs.answer: Add the base rate of the Chapter 76 line and the Section 232 rate (50% or 25%) applied to the full customs value, plus any other Chapter 99 duty that stacks: Section 301 for China (25%), Section 338 for Canadian extrusions and tubes (50%), or Russia's 200%. Since April 6, 2026 the duty is no longer limited to the aluminum content. The 2026 Section 301 and Brazil duties do not stack on Section 232 aluminum. CBP's CSMS # 68253075 explains which 9903.82 heading to report; AD/CVD cash deposits come on top.

faqs.question: What are the Section 232 aluminum smelt and cast requirements?
searchedAs: section 232 aluminum smelt and cast requirements
smelt and cast vs melt and pour
faqs.answer: Importers report, for every Section 232 aluminum entry, the primary and secondary country of smelt (where the largest and second-largest volumes of new aluminum were produced from alumina) and the country of most recent cast (where the aluminum was last liquefied and cast). Steel uses the equivalent "melt and pour" country. The answers decide the UK 25%, U.S.-smelted 10% and Canada/Mexico 25% rates, and the 200% on aluminum smelted or cast in Russia.

faqs.question: Do I need an aluminum import license?
faqs.answer: Yes, for formal entries of unwrought aluminum, extrusions, wire, sheet, foil, tubes, fittings, castings and forgings (7601, 7604–7609, 7616.99.51.60/.70). Commerce's Aluminum Import Monitoring and Analysis (AIM) system issues the license automatically online, with the countries of smelt and cast; the number goes on the entry summary (19 CFR 361.101). Informal entries are exempt, and FTZ admissions need one too.

faqs.question: What is the tariff on aluminum extrusions?
faqs.answer: Extrusions are HTS 7604 (bars, rods and profiles, 1.5% to 5% base) and pay 50% Section 232 from every country; Canadian extrusions 100% (Section 338 adds 50%), Chinese 75% to 80%. Chinese extrusions also carry the 2011 antidumping and countervailing duty orders. Commerce found dumping on extrusions from 14 more countries in 2024, but the ITC voted no injury in November 2024, so no orders were issued.

faqs.question: What are the HS codes and tariffs for aluminum foil, sheet and plate?
searchedAs: is there a tariff on aluminum foil
faqs.answer: Sheet, plate and strip over 0.2 mm thick are HTS 7606 (2.7% to 6.5% base); foil up to 0.2 mm is 7607 (Free to 5.8%). Both pay 50% Section 232. Common alloy sheet from China and 16 other countries, and foil from China, Armenia, Brazil, Oman, Russia and Türkiye, also carry AD/CVD orders. Other aluminum: unwrought 7601, extrusions 7604, wire 7605, tubes 7608, structures and windows 7610, cans 7612, cookware 7615, other articles 7616.

faqs.question: Are there exemptions from the aluminum tariffs, and is scrap covered?
faqs.answer: Very few. Proclamation 10895 ended all country exemptions and quotas on March 12, 2025, and no product exclusion process exists. What remains: the UK 25% (15%), U.S.-smelted derivatives at 10%, Commerce-authorized Canadian and Mexican quantities at 25%, civil aircraft relief for some countries, and goods not on the note 16(c) lists. Aluminum scrap (7602) is not covered: it is Free and on the 2026 Section 301 exemption list, so only China and Brazil (25%) pay extra.

faqs.question: What is the tariff on Russian aluminum?
faqs.answer: 200% under Section 232 (9903.85.67 / 9903.85.68) since March 10, 2023, on top of Russia's column 2 rate or 70% in its place, plus 12.5% Section 301: about 250% to 280% in total. The 200% also applies to aluminum of any other origin that contains primary aluminum smelted in Russia or was cast in Russia (since April 10, 2023), which is why smelt and cast reporting matters.
